title: Do You Need to Join the Local Realtor Board and MLS to Work as an Agent?
metaDesc: Do you need to join the local Realtor board and MLS to work as a Florida real estate agent? Here's what's legally required and what's practically necessary.
h1: Do You Need to Join the Local Realtor Board and MLS to Work as an Agent?
about: Whether Florida real estate agents are required to join the local Realtor board and MLS

hub.name: Become a Real Estate Agent in Florida

answer: No, holding a Florida real estate license doesn’t legally require you to join the local Realtor board or the MLS. But if you plan to actively list and sell homes, you’ll almost always join anyway, because the MLS is how listings actually get shared and found in your market. Referral-only agents, who send clients to active agents instead of listing or showing homes themselves, typically skip both and the dues that come with them.
takeaways: A Florida real estate license comes from the DBPR and doesn’t require Realtor board or MLS membership on its own.
Most actively-selling agents join the local board and MLS anyway, since that’s where listings are entered, searched, and shared with cooperating agents.
Board membership and MLS access usually come as a package, and typically carry their own dues separate from whatever your brokerage charges.
Referral-only agents, who aren’t listing or showing homes, commonly skip board and MLS membership since they don’t need daily access to either.
The right call depends on whether you’ll be actively practicing or holding your license for referrals, so ask your brokerage what’s actually required for your situation.
tldr: You don't legally need to join the local Realtor board or MLS just to hold a Florida real estate license. But if you're actively listing and selling homes, you'll almost always join both, since the MLS is the shared system your market runs on. Referral-only agents, who aren't practicing actively, typically skip both and the dues that come with them.
body:
What Are the Local Realtor Board and the MLS, Exactly?

The local Realtor board (sometimes called a board of Realtors or a regional association) is a membership organization for licensees in a given area. Joining it, along with the state association and the National Association of Realtors, is what lets you use the trademarked title Realtor, which is different from simply holding a real estate license.

The MLS (Multiple Listing Service) is the shared database where active listings in a market get entered, along with details like price, showing instructions, and status. Other agents search the MLS to find homes for their buyers, and public real estate search sites typically pull their listing data from it. In most markets, MLS access is offered through, or tied to, local board membership.

Is Board Membership Legally Required to Hold a Florida License?

No. Your Florida real estate license itself comes from the DBPR (Department of Business and Professional Regulation), and getting or keeping it active doesn’t require you to belong to a Realtor board or have MLS access. You can be a fully licensed, active sales associate under a sponsoring broker without ever joining either one. “Licensed agent” and “Realtor” get used interchangeably in everyday conversation, but legally they aren’t the same thing: one is a state license, the other is a voluntary membership.

So Why Do Most Actively-Selling Agents Join Anyway?

Because the MLS is, practically speaking, the infrastructure your local market runs on. If you’re taking listings, your seller wants that home visible to every buyer’s agent searching the MLS, and if you’re working with buyers, you need to search it yourself to find homes that match what they want. Trying to actively list and sell without MLS access means working with a fraction of the information everyone else in the market has, which makes it very difficult to compete for business.

Since MLS access is usually bundled with, or requires, local board membership, joining the board tends to come along for the ride once you decide to practice actively. Most brokerages that expect production from their agents will assume, and often require, that you carry both.

Who Can Reasonably Skip It?

Agents who hold an active license but aren’t actively listing or showing homes are the clearest exception. This commonly describes referral-only agents, who place their license with a referral-focused brokerage, send clients they know to active agents, and earn a referral fee when a deal closes. Since they’re not entering listings or searching the MLS themselves, there’s little practical reason to pay for access they won’t use.

Agents who are new, part-time, or still deciding how active they’ll be sometimes delay joining as well, until they’re actually ready to take listings or show homes regularly.

What Does It Actually Cost?

Local board dues, state association dues, and NAR dues are usually billed separately from whatever your brokerage charges for desk fees, technology, or training, and MLS access often carries its own additional fee on top of board dues. Combined, these commonly run to several hundred dollars a year, sometimes more depending on the board and market. Exact dues vary by board and change from year to year, so confirm current amounts directly with the local board and your brokerage rather than assuming a fixed figure.

What to Ask Before You Decide

Before assuming you need to join, or that you can skip it, ask your brokerage a few direct questions: Is board and MLS membership required to hold your license there, or optional? Are the dues included in any brokerage fee, or billed to you separately? And if you’re planning to start part-time or on a referral basis, does the brokerage have a track that fits that, without requiring full board and MLS access from day one?

Getting clear answers up front avoids paying for access you won’t use, or discovering later that you needed it and didn’t have it.

Talk It Through With a Local Brokerage

Whether board and MLS membership makes sense for you comes down to how you plan to work, actively listing and selling, or holding your license for referrals while you step back. Adams, Cameron & Co., the area’s largest brokerage since 1963, works with agents across both paths in Volusia and Flagler counties and can walk you through exactly what’s required for the way you want to practice. Start a conversation before you assume either way.

Board, MLS, and association dues vary and change over time; confirm current requirements and costs with the local board and DBPR. Educational only, not legal advice.

faq.q: Do I legally need to join the local Realtor board to hold a Florida real estate license?
faq.a: No. Your license comes from the DBPR and stays active without Realtor board membership. Board membership is what lets you use the title Realtor, which is a separate, voluntary membership rather than a licensing requirement.

faq.q: Can I access the MLS without joining the local Realtor board?
faq.a: In most markets, MLS access is bundled with or requires local board membership, so the two typically come together. A few markets offer separate MLS-only access, but it's uncommon; check with your local board directly.

faq.q: Do referral-only agents need to join the board and MLS?
faq.a: Usually not. Since referral-only agents aren't listing or showing homes themselves, they typically have little practical need for MLS access and often skip both the board and the MLS, along with the associated dues.

faq.q: Are board and MLS dues included in my brokerage fees?
faq.a: Not usually. Local board, state association, and NAR dues, plus any separate MLS access fee, are typically billed to you directly and separately from whatever your brokerage charges for desk fees or technology. Confirm the specifics with your brokerage before joining.
